comments.author: viraptor
comments.text:
Sometimes you have to build something that's not reasonable to fully test while staying profitable. With enough size and scope you end up talking about error budgets instead. I could likely come up with more tests to write for systems at work than I could possibly write in my lifetime. (most will never happen or the user will think "oh weird, I'll just refresh the page") Then there are environment issues: when you start tracking exceptions in the frontend, you will find them, regardless how prepared you were.

Or sure, work harder, do better architecture, build the perfect system, release it in 30 years...

comments.author: Ameo
comments.text:
A lot of this matches my own experience.

My personal feeling is that software quality and bug count are pretty much directly correlated with how you give a shit about it.

For me, it's pretty undeniable that LLMs make it way faster to write code and turn ideas into usable web apps.  But I also find that it's way harder for me to feel much attachment or ownership over the resulting code that gets generated.  When I wrote code by hand, it felt like something that I made, and so my desire to make it good and have it serve as a proxy for my own capability and workmanship was much higher.

Also, once you get into that LLM mode of prompting things into reality, I've also found that it's very hard to drop down into the tedious process of hand-testing the thing that just got created.  The transition from the highly abstract brainstorming and specification process into actually navigating some UI and verifying functionality takes a lot of mental effort for me.

Another area where I've noticed problems is where you had an imperfect understanding of the problem and the best solution differed in reality from what you were imagining during planning.

When coding by hand, I'd usually realize this in the middle of building something out.  I could then step back, undo a few pieces, and proceed with the corrected pattern for the rest of the buildout.  With AI, the AI just plows through, making whatever its interpretation of your prompt work by any means necessary.

So then, you have to try to coax it to make changes to the implementation after the fact to try to bring it in line with your adjusted plan.  And that's the place where antipatterns and other slop often creeps in (2-paragraph tombstone comments explaining the old design in detail and why it was changed, when the old design is no longer relevant at all).

Finally, there's the code review skills, which the author mentions in the article specifically.  This feels very literally like the "how many bugs do you want" thing.  You ever try re-running /code-review xhigh 3-4 times after a big feature buildout?  For me personally, I almost always find 3-4 "real" bugs each time.  The severity often goes down over the iterations, but you'll still read the summary and thing "oh yeah I could imagine that getting hit in practice, I guess".

It's so hard for me to get a measure of how many of these me, or anyone else, would actually run into in production.  And the issue with just applying more and more of these "fixes" is net positive in LoC for the diff; every single one adds more to the sprawl and slop factor of everything.

I guess as a summary here, I just think it's so strange how software dev has changed from writing code and plumbing data to solving these very abstract meta-problems about the code and the software creation process itself.  And everyone using LLMs has their own slightly different version of this, I'm sure, with no real global consensus on the "best" ways to do all of this stuff.

comments.author: nolan
comments.text:
Author here, and yeah I agree with a lot of what you said. I also feel a lot less "ownership" over my AI-authored code, but this eventually morphed into no longer caring about syntax, style, variable names, etc., while still caring a lot about whether the resulting system works or not. If an incident occurs and it's due to something my agent "wrote," then I still feel bad about it, and it motivates me to do better the next time.

You're also right that AI coding results in a lot fewer "aha" moments in the middle of writing the code. Nowadays I might have an agent spit out 3 different full implementations, because in the process of reviewing those implementations I realized something is wrong. This is still faster IMO but it's definitely a different experience. I also still find that I have "shower thoughts" about better designs, so that part hasn't changed.

As for the bugs, yeah: I never try to fix all the bugs, unless I'm feeling particularly masochistic that day. Many of them are true "once in a blue moon" or "cosmic rays" kind of unlikely thing. But since they are almost entirely real bugs, it has given me an appreciation for just how many bugs are likely lurking in software, especially software that hasn't been scrutinized by an LLM.

comments.author: typesanitizer
comments.text:
I'm not really sure if this is true, or rather if this is true, then it's equally true that we you could choose this when knowledge about SQLite and FoundationDB's testing techniques was popularized, or when CompCert/sel4 were created.


My experience is that, in a complex system, you can basically find as many bugs as you ask the agents for. If you get tired of tackling bugs in the PR itself, have no fear: the agent will also find plenty of preexisting bugs for you to spend time on. The question is just when you want to stop and call it “done.”

[...] But the finding of the bugs has become nearly free, and AI agents are also capable of finding very subtle, intricate bugs that otherwise could have flown under the radar for years.


I don't know what kind of systems the author worked on pre-LLMs, but for every system I've worked on, it has always been the case that (1) there were way more open bugs than the team had capacity/willingness/permission etc. to tackle (2) you could basically find various kinds of bugs pretty easily if you were paying attention or stressed the system slightly off the beaten path (this includes compilers!).

If you do an exercise of logging all the bugs you see in week like Dan Luu did (https://danluu.com/everything-is-broken/), if you're paying attention, hitting a few dozen should be fairly easy across all the software you use.

comments.author: nolan
comments.text:
Author here. I've worked on a fairly wide range of open- and closed-source software: database libraries, Android apps, web apps, backend systems, etc. My experience is the same as yours: there are always more bugs than the team has time to work on.

What's changed IMO is that it's much easier to 1) identify the bugs, and 2) root-cause them. I've worked on some bugs where I had a repro and yet even after spending days on it, I couldn't find a valid solution because I couldn't wrap my head around the complexity of the problem. Whereas I've found that agents are spookily good at reasoning things like "if system A has a race condition where it fires after system B when system B was hit with an AbortSignal, then system C would see the state of the database as...", etc.

Maybe the outcome is that we just realize we're even more underwater than we thought, and no more or fewer bugs actually get fixed. But I'd like to think that agents could help us at least prioritize the bugs and fix the criticals/highs much faster.

comments.author: typesanitizer
comments.text:
What's changed IMO is that it's much easier to 1) identify the bugs, and 2) root-cause them. I've worked on some bugs where I had a repro and yet even after spending days on it, I couldn't find a valid solution because I couldn't wrap my head around the complexity of the problem.


I agree with this observation. If I were to reframe my post as a question:

Q: Do you think that a higher speed at finding/triaging bugs would lead to greater control in the hand of engineers in terms of how many bugs get shipped to prod?

I'm curious what you think about the overall effect. My current sense is largely no (similar to what you wrote under "There are still plenty of winds blowing in the opposite direction:") -- as I see it, this is largely controlled by the business tolerance for a bug. If we were to oversimplify and quantify it as a probability p for a change to have a defect, maybe if you have sufficient social capital, you hold the line at p/2 on your team by adding more tests, paying down tech debt etc. But there's still a range -- the amount of investment it would take to get to p/10 or p/100 is likely to get you into trouble.

As one example, I've been in departments where the CI spend per engineer was much higher than many other departments. So even though I felt that we needed more testing, continuous fuzzing etc., asking for more CI infra was not on the table.

comments.author: nolan
comments.text:
The pessimist in me agrees with you: the history of software engineering suggests that "worse is better" always wins, and we'll ship buggy software if we can ship faster.

The optimist in me wonders if the same crowd that thinks the future is neither writing code nor reading it will just buy some CI tool that periodically scans their code, fixes bugs, and merges it unreviewed. If it's seen as just the "cost of doing business" ala Sentry, GitHub Actions, etc., then orgs may pay for it. And honestly it may be better than the status quo.
